When the exit polls closed on this month's midterms, one number should have stopped every pastor in America cold: white evangelicals, nearly a quarter of the presidential electorate just two years ago, made up just 17 percent of the people who actually voted on November 3. That is not a swing. That is an evacuation. And if we want to know why the most churched bloc in American politics keeps missing Election Day, the answer is not in this year's news cycle. It is in 1989.
In January of that year, with George H.W. Bush freshly elected, Jerry Falwell stood before the cameras and announced that he was dissolving the **Moral Majority** -- the organization that had registered millions of voters and helped elect a president. "Our mission is accomplished," he declared. He was stepping back from partisan politics to focus on his church and his college, he said, and he ruled out ever starting a similar political group again.
Consider the full-circle absurdity. In the 1960s, Falwell had preached -- famously, fervently -- that preachers should stay out of politics altogether. In 1979 he reversed himself and built the most feared grassroots machine of the age. In 1989, a decade later, he reversed himself again and went home. One man's career contained the whole movement's future in miniature: mobilize, win, apologize, retreat.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b9fb44ee-c9e6-496b-923f-9d3e409c7c2b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
He was not alone, and the retreat was not quiet. Ten years on, in 1999, two former top lieutenants of the Moral Majority -- columnist Cal Thomas and pastor Ed Dobson -- published 'Blinded by Might: Can the Religious Right Save America?', the most influential work of evangelical political self-criticism ever written. Its argument was not that the religious right had lost. It was that the religious right had been wrong: that mixing Christianity with partisan politics corrupted the church, and that conservative Christians should step back from trying to win the culture wars through political power.
Then there was Billy Graham -- the one figure trusted in every evangelical household -- spending the 1990s publicly distancing himself from politics, and later confessing that he regretted his closeness to Richard Nixon and wished he had "steered clear of politics" entirely.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/2a59c020-6498-483a-8a41-e070be0dc30a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Assemble the signals -- the founder disbanding his machine, his lieutenants renouncing the cause in a bestseller, the movement's most beloved elder apologizing for having engaged at all -- and you have the clearest, most repeated message American Christianity received in the late twentieth century: politics is dirty; good men withdraw; the church's calling lies elsewhere.
The pews took the message literally. Three decades later, we are staring at the result.
**The harvest of the retreat**
Here is the harvest. By estimates that circulate through every Christian mobilization ministry in the country, roughly 40 million self-identified Christians typically sit out American elections, and some 15 million Christian citizens are not even _registered_ to vote. In 2024, the research team at Arizona Christian University -- under George Barna, the man who practically invented evangelical polling -- projected that 32 million regular churchgoers would stay home that November, and found that barely more than half of America's Christian churches had taken even the simplest election-related step of encouraging their people to vote. Fewer still taught their congregations anything about the candidates or the stakes. In midterms, roughly four in ten faith voters do not show up at all.
The trajectory is falling, not standing still. Evangelical votes cast peaked at 44.4 million in 2020, then dropped 20 percent by 2024, to 35.5 million -- a decline that should have triggered national soul-searching in every denomination and instead passed mostly in silence. Now comes the sequel: a white evangelical share of the midterm electorate down eight points in two years, from a quarter of all voters to less than a fifth.
You cannot spend thirty years telling a body of believers that politics corrupts and then act surprised when the body stops voting. Sermons shape defaults; defaults shape habits; habits become an electorate. A generation was discipled, week after week, from the most respected platforms in evangelical life, to believe that the ballot box was someone else's battlefield. They obeyed. What we now call "extremely low Christian turnout" is not a mystery or a demographic accident. It is obedience to three decades of instruction.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/2df602b3-1899-4da4-9033-e2338a1cd876?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**The one who stayed**
Now consider the man everyone laughed at. Pat Robertson never got an apology tour. He ran for president in 1988, finished second in Iowa, and was treated ever after as an embarrassment -- but his campaign taught evangelicals how precinct caucuses actually work, and out of its leftover machinery he built the Christian Coalition, the most effective grassroots operation religious America has ever produced: voter guides and election literature by the tens of millions, stuffed into pews on the eve of elections; school-board candidates recruited; precinct maps filled county by county. On 'The 700 Club', night after night, he did what Falwell, Thomas, Dobson and Graham had stopped doing -- he told religious conservatives that elections, judges and legislatures were their business, and that staying home was not neutrality but surrender.
History's verdict on Robertson remains unsettled, and plenty of his statements earned the mockery. But on the one question this column is about -- whether Christians should organize and vote -- he was right, the respectable men who retreated were wrong, and the numbers above are the receipt.
Before September 10, 2025, Turning Point USA was the most effective youth political machine either party has built in the modern era: a 18-year-old with seed money from Foster Friess turned it into 3,500 chapters, an $85-million-a-year operation, AmericaFest packing twenty thousand people, a top-ranked podcast, and a ballot operation credited with moving young men to Trump in 2024. Kirk himself was the connective tissue of the whole right -- pastors, podcasters, senators, White House officials all passed through his orbit, and nobody else had that Rolodex at 31.
Then came the assassination, and the martyrdom surge: memorial crowds in the tens of thousands, tens of thousands of chapter inquiries within days, a million donors, college chapters up 64 percent, high school chapters nearly tripled, more money raised this year than in the entire 2024 cycle. On paper, TPUSA/Faith is bigger than it was the day he died.
But the drop off is real where it counts -- the energy. What made TPUSA electric was never the chapter count. It was the man in the open-air tent, mic in hand, taking the hardest questions a hostile campus could throw and turning it into clips that flooded every feed by Monday morning. That engine ran on his instincts, his speed, his willingness to stand in the fire week after week. No successor replicates it, and everyone knows it. What's left is an institution with more chapters and less electricity -- student leaders describing a void, a divided landscape, feuds around the family, and a pivot toward 2028 kingmaking because elections are measurable and charisma isn't.
Erika Kirk has been a genuinely useful face for the grief phase, but grief phases end. Organizations built around one man's talent either find the next one or become a museum of him. Right now TPUSA is raising more money than ever to answer a question Charlie never had to ask: what is it for, when the reason people showed up is gone?
**What the retreat bought**
Thomas and Dobson were right that politics cannot save souls, right that a movement can come to love its power more than its Lord, right that the church was diminished when it looked like a party auxiliary. If the choice were between a politicized church and a purified one, I would take the purified one.
But that was never the choice on offer. Withdrawal did not purify the culture; it vacated it. The real choice was between engaged Christians and everyone else -- and in a democracy, everyone else shows up. While the retreat preachers went home, the other side organized: school boards, county parties, statehouses, courts. A vacuum does not stay empty. It fills with people who were never told to leave the field.
Here is the empirical embarrassment for the retreat thesis: every major victory the religious right claims was won by the wing that refused to retreat. Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization did not descend from heaven in 2022. It was built across three decades of sustained engagement -- judicial nominations confirmed by senators, legal movements funded, state legislatures stocked precinct by precinct -- by exactly the political persistence that **Blinded by Might** declared a corruption. The engaged tradition delivered the one thing the movement had promised its people for fifty years. The retreat tradition contributed nothing to it except the thinning of the ranks now needed to defend the victory after it was won.
That is the cruel arithmetic of the moment. You can win a Supreme Court majority and then lose the Senate that confirms its successors. You can win a statehouse and lose it in a midterm when four in ten of your own faith sit home because, a generation ago, someone famous told them politics is filthy. Retreat did not merely fail to win anything. It failed to keep what engagement had won.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/388617b9-1be0-4a6e-aab6-eab3e8c41676?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**The mission was not accomplished**
Falwell's phrase deserves its epitaph. "Our mission is accomplished" was spoken in January 1989, when the Supreme Court still blessed abortion on demand, organized school prayer was still banned, and every institution the movement cared about remained in hostile hands -- problems Falwell himself admitted still persisted. _Nothing_ was accomplished. What had happened was that a president had been elected, which was the beginning of the work, not the end of it. The man who understood that work better than anyone concluded it and went home, taking the movement's permission structure with him. Every pastor reading the news drew the obvious lesson: if Falwell is out, why am I in?
The remedy is not a mystery, and it is not a new organization. It is a return to the plain things the Christian Coalition once did, done now by churches themselves: registration tables in the lobbies, sermons that treat citizenship as part of stewardship rather than a concession to the flesh, plain speech about the stakes on the actual ballot, and the patient, unglamorous labor of precinct politics that Robertson's people once performed and almost no one performs now.
Christianity remains, by an order of magnitude, the largest faith in this country. If its voters turned out at the rate of its own stated convictions, no American election would ever again be close enough to dispute. They do not turn out, and the reason is not apathy. It is discipleship -- three decades of it, pointing the other way. The retreat preachers got their wish. The question for 2028 is whether the pews will finally stop honoring it.

What the retreat bought Thomas and Dobson were right that politics cannot save souls, right that a movement can come to love its power more than its Lord, right that the church was diminished when it looked like a party auxiliary. If the choice were between a politicized church and a purified one, I would take the purified one. But that was never the choice on offer. Withdrawal did not purify the culture; it vacated it. The real choice was between engaged Christians and everyone else -- and in a democracy, everyone else shows up. While the retreat preachers went home, the other side organized: school boards, county parties, statehouses, courts. A vacuum does not stay empty. It fills with people who were never told to leave the field. Here is the empirical embarrassment for the retreat thesis: every major victory the religious right claims was won by the wing that refused to retreat. Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization did not descend from heaven in 2022. It was built across three decades of sustained engagement -- judicial nominations confirmed by senators, legal movements funded, state legislatures stocked precinct by precinct -- by exactly the political persistence that Blinded by Might declared a corruption. The engaged tradition delivered the one thing the movement had promised its people for fifty years. The retreat tradition contributed nothing to it except the thinning of the ranks now needed to defend the victory after it was won. That is the cruel arithmetic of the moment. You can win a Supreme Court majority and then lose the Senate that confirms its successors. You can win a statehouse and lose it in a midterm when four in ten of your own faith sit home because, a generation ago, someone famous told them politics is filthy. Retreat did not merely fail to win anything. It failed to keep what engagement had won. | | ---|---|--- The mission was not accomplished Falwell's phrase deserves its epitaph. "Our mission is accomplished" was spoken in January 1989, when the Supreme Court still blessed abortion on demand, organized school prayer was still banned, and every institution the movement cared about remained in hostile hands -- problems Falwell himself admitted still persisted. Nothing was accomplished. What had happened was that a president had been elected, which was the beginning of the work, not the end of it. The man who understood that work better than anyone concluded it and went home, taking the movement's permission structure with him. Every pastor reading the news drew the obvious lesson: if Falwell is out, why am I in? The remedy is not a mystery, and it is not a new organization. It is a return to the plain things the Christian Coalition once did, done now by churches themselves: registration tables in the lobbies, sermons that treat citizenship as part of stewardship rather than a concession to the flesh, plain speech about the stakes on the actual ballot, and the patient, unglamorous labor of precinct politics that Robertson's people once performed and almost no one performs now. Christianity remains, by an order of magnitude, the largest faith in this country. If its voters turned out at the rate of its own stated convictions, no American election would ever again be close enough to dispute. They do not turn out, and the reason is not apathy. It is discipleship -- three decades of it, pointing the other way. The retreat preachers got their wish. The question for 2028 is whether the pews will finally stop honoring it. | | ---|---|--- You're currently a free subscriber to . | | | It's Chuck Schumer.

Against all odds, Democrats have won the majority.

This is a generational remake of the Senate map. So far, we've managed to flip **_eight seats_** ‐‐ Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas ‐‐ all while defending Michigan, New Hampshire, Georgia, and _every other Democratic‐held seat._

**And we're not done yet:** Right now, the race in Alaska is still too close to call, and we could expand our new majority.

I have five words for the American people as we head into this new era: **Relief is on the way.**

You showed up to the polls to put a check on Donald Trump, his allies, and their agenda ‐‐ so my fellow Democrats and I are going to do our part. We are going to stand up to Trump's chaos, crack down on corruption, and work hard to drive down costs ‐‐ _the president can work with us if he chooses, or face another drubbing for his party in 2028._

This historic victory wouldn't have been possible without the support of dedicated Democrats like you. So from the bottom of my heart, thank you for showing up when it mattered, and for putting in the work to make our country a better place.

**Now, we need to keep this momentum going as we head into 2028. Republicans won't stop fighting, so we have to do everything in our power to defend the majority we worked so hard for.**

Last month, I traveled to Geneva, Switzerland, to participate in the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) Climate Change Study Programme.
For five days, I sat with scientists, economists, international policy experts, and professionals from around the world, learning from people working within the institutions responsible for confronting the greatest environmental crisis in human history.
We discussed the physics of a warming planet, the economics of adaptation, the legal obligations of governments, the human costs of disasters, and the enormous gap between what nations have promised and what they have delivered.
I came to Geneva as an environmental scientist who has spent much of my career working at the intersection of climate change, disaster response, and government accountability. I wasn't expecting to learn that climate change is dangerous. I've spent years studying and documenting those dangers.
What interested me was something else: **What happens to the science after scientists hand it to the people responsible for acting on it?**
That question followed me from the World Meteorological Organization to discussions with representatives of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the International Labour Organization, the UN Environment Programme, the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, and other institutions.
Now, as representatives from around the world gather in Antalya, Turkiye, for[ COP31](https://substack.com/redirect/fcd026aa-eeac-4de1-b4f1-d459de567581?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the answer has never been more consequential.
The science is increasingly precise. The technology is improving. The economic case for action is overwhelming.
And the world is still moving dangerously slowly.
## **1\. The climate crisis is no longer a projection of the future. It 's a measurement of right now.**
Most of our sessions took place at the World Meteorological Organization, the Geneva-based institution that coordinates international meteorological observations and climate information.
For a geographer and climatologist, there was something extraordinary about being in a building so closely connected to the world's climate monitoring infrastructure and the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).](https://substack.com/redirect/3a82347d-7056-47ef-acf1-7fc9bc00a3f7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Our first presentation focused on something fundamental to science: how we know what we know.
Climate observations come from multiple independent sources. Surface stations, ocean measurements, satellites, and historical records are assembled into datasets that allow scientists to reconstruct how Earth's climate has changed.
Those independent datasets converge on the same conclusion: Earth is warming rapidly.
Bringing the point home, WMO released its 2026 State of the Climate update on the heels of our progam.
The [findings](https://substack.com/redirect/5fa419bb-ad97-481f-ac6e-ba995a3cf6c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) were staggering.
The global average temperature from January through September 2026 was approximately 1.47°C above the preindustrial average. **The past 12 years are expected to be the 12 warmest on record.**
Ocean heat and global mean sea level have reached record highs. A strengthening El Niño threatens to intensify extreme heat, drought, and heavy rainfall into 2027.
These aren't speculative projections. They are observations of a planet already undergoing profound physical changes.
And they are unfolding against an increasingly troubling political backdrop.
The [UN Environment Programme's 2026 Emissions Gap Report ](https://substack.com/redirect/abd85895-74b1-44da-b4be-4f1bac92453d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)estimates that existing government policies put the world on a trajectory toward approximately **2.8 °C of warming this century**.
Even if countries fully implement their current national climate commitments, projected warming remains around 2.6°C.
The difference between 1.5°C and 2.8°C is not a minor adjustment to the thermostat. It means substantially greater risks to human health, food production, ecosystems, water supplies, and the habitability of entire regions.
It means mass displacement, migration, disease, disasters and death.
The question is no longer whether we have enough evidence to act.
It's why the evidence has failed to produce an adequate response.

## **2\. Disasters aren 't simply natural. Vulnerability is built into them.**
With the [UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction](https://substack.com/redirect/e2afb367-42cd-4381-a32e-3680360716e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), our discussions turned to one of the most important distinctions in disaster science.
A hazard is not the same thing as a disaster.
A hurricane can pass over two communities with nearly identical winds and rainfall, yet produce radically different outcomes. Hurricane Katrina illustrated that point in stark contrast.
The difference often lies in exposure and vulnerability: where people live, the infrastructure protecting them, their access to healthcare and transportation, the reliability of warning systems, and the resources available for evacuation and recovery.
This is central to the [Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction](https://substack.com/redirect/1c795202-ce50-41d7-87a1-1af27b57c680?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), the international agreement guiding efforts to prevent and reduce disaster losses.
UNDRR representatives explained why climate adaptation cannot focus exclusively on changes in the physical hazard.
We must also change the social, economic, and political conditions that turn hazardous events into human catastrophes.
That distinction matters enormously in the United States.
When a hurricane strikes a wealthy coastal neighborhood, homeowners may have insurance, reliable transportation, and the financial means to relocate.
A low-income family living in a flood-prone rental property may have none of those protections.
The storm is the same. The disaster isn't.
The same principle applies internationally.
Countries already burdened by poverty, inadequate infrastructure, political instability, or debt often have the fewest resources to protect themselves against climate impacts, despite contributing comparatively little to the emissions responsible for warming.
And disasters can create vicious cycles. Infrastructure is destroyed, government revenues decline, reconstruction costs rise, and resources that could have been invested in prevention are diverted into recovery.
In Geneva, the message was clear: disaster risk reduction must be built into development decisions before catastrophe strikes.
_A disaster is not just a test of the weather. It is a test of the systems we built before the weather arrived._

## **3\. Climate finance: The countries least responsible are paying the highest price.**
If one subject connected nearly every discussion in Geneva, it was money.
Climate action requires enormous investments in clean energy, resilient infrastructure, water systems, public health, agriculture, and disaster preparedness.
But the central problem is not simply the total amount of money available.
It is who controls it, who receives it, and under what conditions.
In our climate finance sessions, representatives discussed the responsibilities of governments, development banks, commercial financial institutions, and international funding mechanisms.
The discussions repeatedly returned to countries that face enormous climate risks while struggling with debt and limited institutional capacity.
A developing country may need financing to protect its coastline, strengthen its electric grid, or build an early-warning system.
But if that funding arrives primarily as loans, the country may be forced to assume additional debt to protect itself against damage caused disproportionately by emissions from wealthier nations.
The injustice is difficult to overstate.
And the latest numbers make it impossible to ignore.
According to UNEP's 2026 [Adaptation Gap Report](https://substack.com/redirect/922dffb9-41a4-4503-846c-ba27c4b9da06?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), international public adaptation finance to developing countries reached approximately $28.2 to $31.7 billion in 2024.
Estimated adaptation needs, meanwhile, are approximately **$305 billion annually by 2035**.
Even tripling international public adaptation finance would meet only about 20-29% of projected needs.
At COP31, this is not merely an academic discussion.
On November 13, UN climate chief Simon Stiell [warned that developing countries are being trapped in a cycle of debt, disasters, and increasingly expensive borrowing.](https://substack.com/redirect/2777efab-2169-467f-ab60-8b58a7546c7b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
He called for financing that strengthens national institutions, reduces barriers to accessing funds, and recognizes that grants and highly concessional financing remain essential for vulnerable countries.
This closely echoes what we discussed in Geneva.
Climate finance cannot be judged solely by how much money wealthy nations announce at international conferences.
It must also be judged by how much reaches the communities that need it, how quickly it arrives, and whether it leaves those communities better equipped to withstand the next disaster.
Financing climate adaptation by deepening the debts of climate-vulnerable countries is not a sustainable solution.
It is another way of transferring the costs of the crisis to those least responsible for creating it.

## **4\. Climate change is a human rights crisis.**
One of the most consequential sessions I attended was led by a representative of the [Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.](https://substack.com/redirect/8a1ae7fd-db67-4db9-9348-e2e0e26e396f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The central argument was straightforward: climate change is not merely an environmental problem.
It is a human rights problem.
The consequences of climate change threaten access to clean water, adequate food, housing, healthcare, livelihoods, and, in extreme circumstances, life itself.
A human rights-based approach therefore changes how climate policies should be evaluated.
It isn't enough for a government to announce an emissions reduction target.
We must also ask whether the policy protects vulnerable communities, respects Indigenous rights, includes affected populations in decision-making, and provides meaningful accountability.
The session also examined the risks of climate policies that reproduce existing inequalities.
A renewable energy project, for example, may reduce greenhouse gas emissions while displacing communities or violating land rights.
A carbon market may produce accounting credits without delivering meaningful benefits to the people living where the project operates.
A government may celebrate a climate finance commitment while the communities most exposed to flooding, drought, or extreme heat remain unable to access assistance.
The human rights discussion challenged us to consider not only whether climate action works, but _for whom it works._
This is especially relevant as countries negotiate the next stages of implementing the [Paris Agreement.](https://substack.com/redirect/4e282b23-2e4c-4e48-9002-003987e5d228?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Human rights cannot be an optional consideration added after a climate policy has already been designed.
They must be part of the design itself.

## **5\. The green transition cannot leave workers behind.**
With guests from the [International Labour Organization](https://substack.com/redirect/914ff589-eda3-4ab5-a030-53b5e14fda52?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), our discussion focused on a deceptively simple question:
What happens to workers when the economy changes?
A transition away from fossil fuels will reshape employment across energy, transportation, manufacturing, agriculture, construction, and other industries.
Some jobs will disappear. Others will emerge. Many will require new skills.
A successful transition cannot be measured exclusively by the number of solar panels installed or coal plants retired.
We must also account for wages, working conditions, social protections, retraining opportunities, and the economic security of communities whose livelihoods depend on industries undergoing transformation.
The ILO describes this as a _[just transition](https://substack.com/redirect/024ff2ba-f898-4895-816a-4e54908c3bfc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[.](https://substack.com/redirect/024ff2ba-f898-4895-816a-4e54908c3bfc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Its [2026 COP31 briefing ](https://substack.com/redirect/616bbf15-7e3d-4287-a821-4a8d9a7dec36?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)estimates that at least 2.4 billion workers worldwide are exposed to excessive heat.
By 2030, heat stress could eliminate the equivalent of[ 80 million full-time jobs](https://substack.com/redirect/084c18cb-1d2e-42f0-9985-b0d56c624eac?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
At the same time, renewable energy already supported approximately [16.6 million jobs globally in 2025.](https://substack.com/redirect/e1469e01-bfdd-4d6f-9c41-c83dacfee911?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Those figures reveal two sides of the same transformation.
Climate change is already damaging workers' health and productivity. Climate action, meanwhile, can generate new employment and economic opportunities.
But neither outcome is distributed equally.
Without deliberate policies, the benefits of new industries may accumulate among investors and highly skilled workers while vulnerable communities bear the costs of transition.
The ILO's framework emphasizes worker participation, social dialogue, collective bargaining, skills development, and decent work.
The lesson is particularly important in countries where climate policy is routinely framed as a choice between protecting jobs and protecting the environment.
That is a false choice.
The real challenge is designing policies that protect both workers and the planet.

## **6\. Water connects nearly every dimension of the climate crisis.**
With guests from [UN-Water](https://substack.com/redirect/d4f3d382-7855-4412-8a81-177f884a8ed2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), we examined the climate crisis through a resource so fundamental that nearly every human activity depends on it:
Water.
Climate change is altering when precipitation falls, how intensely it falls, where water is stored, and how reliably communities can access it.
Some regions face increasingly severe droughts. Others experience destructive flooding. Many experience both.
Glaciers and mountain snowpack, which provide seasonal freshwater supplies to millions of people, are changing rapidly.
Rising seas threaten coastal aquifers with saltwater intrusion.
And extreme weather can overwhelm water treatment systems, damage sanitation infrastructure, and increase exposure to waterborne disease.
[One example](https://substack.com/redirect/e268f60c-afd9-4977-999d-0de941b57bfc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) discussed in Geneva involved the recent destructive flooding caused by glacial melt in the Himalayan mountains, causing more than 1,000 deaths in Nepal and Tibet.[ I wrote about that here.](https://substack.com/redirect/d331e7a3-98b9-4fd5-836c-98d825283a32?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The broader lesson was that climate impacts do not respect the boundaries we draw between sectors or political jurisdictions.
A mountain glacier affects a river. A river affects a reservoir. A reservoir affects agriculture, electricity generation, drinking water, and public health.
The people making decisions about each of those systems may work in entirely different institutions.
This is one reason UN-Water exists as a coordination mechanism across the UN system.
And it is why water security must become central to climate adaptation rather than treated as a secondary environmental issue.
At COP31, [UNEP has highlighted the Baku Dialogue on Water for Climate Action](https://substack.com/redirect/0c700e33-bacb-4dac-b0bb-350d6e060cba?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), an international initiative connecting climate policy, finance, and water management.
The challenge is no longer simply understanding the hydrological consequences of climate change -- it is ensuring that water governance, infrastructure investment, and climate policy respond to those consequences together.

## **7\. Technology can help solve the crisis. It can also make it worse.**
One of the more interesting sessions during the week examined the growing role of digital technology and artificial intelligence in climate action.
Digital systems can improve weather forecasting, support early warnings, optimize energy networks, monitor environmental changes, and strengthen disaster response.
Satellite observations and advanced computational models have already transformed our ability to understand the Earth system.
But technology is not environmentally neutral.
Data centers consume electricity and water. Manufacturing electronics requires minerals, energy, and industrial infrastructure. Digital devices generate growing quantities of electronic waste.
Artificial intelligence adds another layer of complexity.
Its computational demands can create new pressures on energy and water systems even as its applications promise greater efficiency elsewhere.
This tension should be central to how governments evaluate emerging technologies.
A technology that improves efficiency in one sector may still create substantial environmental costs through its infrastructure, supply chains, or rapid expansion.
The relevant question is not whether AI is inherently good or bad for the climate.
It is whether particular applications deliver measurable environmental and social benefits that outweigh their full lifecycle costs.
The same principle applies to corporate sustainability claims.
In our sessions on environmental, social, and governance reporting, we examined how companies disclose their environmental performance, and how those disclosures can obscure as much as they reveal.
A corporation may publish an attractive sustainability report while its core business model continues to depend on environmentally destructive practices.
Transparency is essential, but disclosure is not the same thing as accountability.
And neither is a substitute for measurable emissions reductions.

## **8\. Climate change is part of a larger planetary crisis.**
One of the most important ideas presented by [UNEP](https://substack.com/redirect/51dad55c-c7e4-43c0-aeaf-631fdc3fa87f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was that climate change cannot be separated from biodiversity loss and pollution.
Together, these form what the UN calls the _[triple planetary crisis](https://substack.com/redirect/331c878c-fdc6-4911-ba3f-31368aaa5d72?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_[.](https://substack.com/redirect/331c878c-fdc6-4911-ba3f-31368aaa5d72?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Deforestation contributes to climate change while destroying habitats and weakening ecosystems that store carbon and regulate water.
Pollution damages human health and biodiversity while imposing enormous economic costs.
Resource extraction can accelerate environmental degradation even when the resulting materials are used in technologies intended to reduce emissions.
This is why climate solutions must be evaluated as parts of larger systems.
Replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy is essential. But an energy transition that ignores destructive mining practices, resource consumption, labor exploitation, and ecological damage risks reproducing other dimensions of the crisis.
The discussions on circular economies, sustainable procurement, and systems thinking emphasized reducing waste, improving resource efficiency, and designing economic activity around ecological limits.
The ultimate goal is not simply to preserve today's patterns of consumption while changing the technologies that power them -- it is to build economies capable of supporting human well-being without continually degrading the natural systems on which that well-being depends.

## **9\. International climate agreements are only as powerful as their implementation.**
During the [UNFCCC](https://substack.com/redirect/b27e851c-1de0-400e-b23f-61673435031b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) session, we examined the architecture of international climate governance.
The [1992 Framework Convention](https://substack.com/redirect/8bc6a0bb-16cc-4d54-8da0-957327089e62?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) established the foundation for global cooperation.
The 1997[ Kyoto Protocol ](https://substack.com/redirect/d41a48c5-50d7-4a06-be6c-69e89715f94c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)introduced binding emissions targets for certain developed countries.
The [2016 Paris Agreement](https://substack.com/redirect/4e282b23-2e4c-4e48-9002-003987e5d228?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) created a broader framework in which countries submit and periodically strengthen their national climate commitments.
One principle runs throughout these agreements: _common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities_.
In practical terms, countries share responsibility for confronting climate change, but they have not contributed equally to the problem and do not possess equal resources to address it.
This principle is fundamental to international climate negotiations.
It is also a source of persistent political conflict.
Countries disagree over how much they should reduce emissions, who should pay for adaptation, how historical responsibility should influence present obligations, and what mechanisms should exist to ensure accountability.
Meanwhile, the atmosphere continues accumulating greenhouse gases.
The latest [UNEP Emissions Gap Report](https://substack.com/redirect/abd85895-74b1-44da-b4be-4f1bac92453d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) makes the implementation problem painfully clear.
_Even full implementation of existing national commitments would leave the world on a dangerous warming trajectory._
At COP31, negotiators are debating how to strengthen mitigation, adaptation, financing, and the mechanisms used to evaluate progress.
But agreements alone do not cool the planet.
Emissions reductions do.
And the distance between diplomatic promises and physical outcomes is where the future of climate policy will be decided.

## **10\. The biggest lesson from Geneva: We know far more than we are willing to do.**
One of the questions posed to us during the programme was what we intended to do with the knowledge we gained.
It is a question that deserves to be asked of governments, corporations, and international institutions as well.
What happens after the conference ends?
After the speeches, presentations, negotiations, and photographs?
After the next set of commitments is announced?
I left Geneva with a deeper appreciation for the extraordinary expertise distributed throughout the UN system.
Scientists are monitoring changes in the Earth system with remarkable precision.
Disaster specialists understand how to reduce exposure and vulnerability.
Economists are developing mechanisms to finance resilience.
Human rights experts are identifying legal responsibilities.
Labor specialists are designing frameworks for equitable transitions.
Engineers and technology experts are developing practical tools for reducing emissions and protecting communities.
None of these disciplines can solve the crisis alone.
That was perhaps the most consistent lesson across the programme.
Climate change is not simply a problem of atmospheric chemistry. It is a problem of energy, economics, governance, public health, human rights, infrastructure, and political power.
The challenge is not a shortage of knowledge, but rather the failure to translate that knowledge into coordinated, adequately financed, enforceable action.
As COP31 continues in Turkiye, governments have another opportunity to narrow the distance between what they know and what they do.
But the atmosphere does not negotiate. The oceans do not recognize political boundaries. And communities facing deadly heat, rising seas, and destructive storms cannot wait for another decade of incremental promises.
The people I met in Geneva are working on different parts of an extraordinarily complex problem.
Their work matters.
But the ultimate measure of success will not be how many conferences are held, how many reports are published, or how many commitments are announced.
It will be whether emissions fall, whether ecosystems recover, whether vulnerable communities become safer, and whether governments finally accept responsibility for the future their decisions are creating.
We already have the warning. We already have much of the knowledge. And we already have many of the tools.
What remains is the choice to use them.

Mesoscale News is reader-supported, independent journalism. Your paid subscription helps me continue investigating the intersection of science, climate, public health, and political power, without corporate sponsors or political gatekeepers. If you believe this work matters, please consider becoming a paid subscriber. Every subscription helps keep independent science reporting alive. Last month, I traveled to Geneva, Switzerland, to participate in the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) Climate Change Study Programme. For five days, I sat with scientists, economists, international policy experts, and professionals from around the world, learning from people working within the institutions responsible for confronting the greatest environmental crisis in human history. We discussed the physics of a warming planet, the economics of adaptation, the legal obligations of governments, the human costs of disasters, and the enormous gap between what nations have promised and what they have delivered. I came to Geneva as an environmental scientist who has spent much of my career working at the intersection of climate change, disaster response, and government accountability. I wasn't expecting to learn that climate change is dangerous. I've spent years studying and documenting those dangers. What interested me was something else: What happens to the science after scientists hand it to the people responsible for acting on it? That question followed me from the World Meteorological Organization to discussions with representatives of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the International Labour Organization, the UN Environment Programme, the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, and other institutions. Now, as representatives from around the world gather in Antalya, Turkiye, for, the answer has never been more consequential. The science is increasingly precise. The technology is improving. The economic case for action is overwhelming. And the world is still moving dangerously slowly. 1\. The climate crisis is no longer a projection of the future. It 's a measurement of right now. Most of our sessions took place at the World Meteorological Organization, the Geneva-based institution that coordinates international meteorological observations and climate information. For a geographer and climatologist, there was something extraordinary about being in a building so closely connected to the world's climate monitoring infrastructure and the Our first presentation focused on something fundamental to science: how we know what we know. Climate observations come from multiple independent sources. Surface stations, ocean measurements, satellites, and historical records are assembled into datasets that allow scientists to reconstruct how Earth's climate has changed. Those independent datasets converge on the same conclusion: Earth is warming rapidly. Bringing the point home, WMO released its 2026 State of the Climate update on the heels of our progam. The were staggering. The global average temperature from January through September 2026 was approximately 1.47°C above the preindustrial average. The past 12 years are expected to be the 12 warmest on record. Ocean heat and global mean sea level have reached record highs. A strengthening El Niño threatens to intensify extreme heat, drought, and heavy rainfall into 2027. These aren't speculative projections. They are observations of a planet already undergoing profound physical changes. And they are unfolding against an increasingly troubling political backdrop. The that existing government policies put the world on a trajectory toward approximately 2.8 °C of warming this century. Even if countries fully implement their current national climate commitments, projected warming remains around 2.6°C. The difference between 1.5°C and 2.8°C is not a minor adjustment to the thermostat. It means substantially greater risks to human health, food production, ecosystems, water supplies, and the habitability of entire regions. It means mass displacement, migration, disease, disasters and death. The question is no longer whether we have enough evidence to act. It's why the evidence has failed to produce an adequate response. 2\. Disasters aren 't simply natural. Vulnerability is built into them. With the , our discussions turned to one of the most important distinctions in disaster science. A hazard is not the same thing as a disaster. A hurricane can pass over two communities with nearly identical winds and rainfall, yet produce radically different outcomes. Hurricane Katrina illustrated that point in stark contrast. The difference often lies in exposure and vulnerability: where people live, the infrastructure protecting them, their access to healthcare and transportation, the reliability of warning systems, and the resources available for evacuation and recovery. This is central to the , the international agreement guiding efforts to prevent and reduce disaster losses. UNDRR representatives explained why climate adaptation cannot focus exclusively on changes in the physical hazard. We must also change the social, economic, and political conditions that turn hazardous events into human catastrophes. That distinction matters enormously in the United States. When a hurricane strikes a wealthy coastal neighborhood, homeowners may have insurance, reliable transportation, and the financial means to relocate. A low-income family living in a flood-prone rental property may have none of those protections. The storm is the same. The disaster isn't. The same principle applies internationally. Countries already burdened by poverty, inadequate infrastructure, political instability, or debt often have the fewest resources to protect themselves against climate impacts, despite contributing comparatively little to the emissions responsible for warming. And disasters can create vicious cycles. Infrastructure is destroyed, government revenues decline, reconstruction costs rise, and resources that could have been invested in prevention are diverted into recovery. In Geneva, the message was clear: disaster risk reduction must be built into development decisions before catastrophe strikes. A disaster is not just a test of the weather. It is a test of the systems we built before the weather arrived. 3\. Climate finance: The countries least responsible are paying the highest price. If one subject connected nearly every discussion in Geneva, it was money. Climate action requires enormous investments in clean energy, resilient infrastructure, water systems, public health, agriculture, and disaster preparedness. But the central problem is not simply the total amount of money available. It is who controls it, who receives it, and under what conditions. In our climate finance sessions, representatives discussed the responsibilities of governments, development banks, commercial financial institutions, and international funding mechanisms. The discussions repeatedly returned to countries that face enormous climate risks while struggling with debt and limited institutional capacity. A developing country may need financing to protect its coastline, strengthen its electric grid, or build an early-warning system. But if that funding arrives primarily as loans, the country may be forced to assume additional debt to protect itself against damage caused disproportionately by emissions from wealthier nations. The injustice is difficult to overstate. And the latest numbers make it impossible to ignore. According to UNEP's 2026 , international public adaptation finance to developing countries reached approximately $28.2 to $31.7 billion in 2024. Estimated adaptation needs, meanwhile, are approximately $305 billion annually by 2035. Even tripling international public adaptation finance would meet only about 20-29% of projected needs. At COP31, this is not merely an academic discussion. On November 13, UN climate chief Simon Stiell He called for financing that strengthens national institutions, reduces barriers to accessing funds, and recognizes that grants and highly concessional financing remain essential for vulnerable countries. This closely echoes what we discussed in Geneva. Climate finance cannot be judged solely by how much money wealthy nations announce at international conferences. It must also be judged by how much reaches the communities that need it, how quickly it arrives, and whether it leaves those communities better equipped to withstand the next disaster. Financing climate adaptation by deepening the debts of climate-vulnerable countries is not a sustainable solution. It is another way of transferring the costs of the crisis to those least responsible for creating it. 4\. Climate change is a human rights crisis. One of the most consequential sessions I attended was led by a representative of the The central argument was straightforward: climate change is not merely an environmental problem. It is a human rights problem. The consequences of climate change threaten access to clean water, adequate food, housing, healthcare, livelihoods, and, in extreme circumstances, life itself. A human rights-based approach therefore changes how climate policies should be evaluated. It isn't enough for a government to announce an emissions reduction target. We must also ask whether the policy protects vulnerable communities, respects Indigenous rights, includes affected populations in decision-making, and provides meaningful accountability. The session also examined the risks of climate policies that reproduce existing inequalities. A renewable energy project, for example, may reduce greenhouse gas emissions while displacing communities or violating land rights. A carbon market may produce accounting credits without delivering meaningful benefits to the people living where the project operates. A government may celebrate a climate finance commitment while the communities most exposed to flooding, drought, or extreme heat remain unable to access assistance. The human rights discussion challenged us to consider not only whether climate action works, but for whom it works. This is especially relevant as countries negotiate the next stages of implementing the Human rights cannot be an optional consideration added after a climate policy has already been designed. They must be part of the design itself. 5\. The green transition cannot leave workers behind. With guests from the , our discussion focused on a deceptively simple question: What happens to workers when the economy changes? A transition away from fossil fuels will reshape employment across energy, transportation, manufacturing, agriculture, construction, and other industries. Some jobs will disappear. Others will emerge. Many will require new skills. A successful transition cannot be measured exclusively by the number of solar panels installed or coal plants retired. We must also account for wages, working conditions, social protections, retraining opportunities, and the economic security of communities whose livelihoods depend on industries undergoing transformation. The ILO describes this as a Its that at least 2.4 billion workers worldwide are exposed to excessive heat. By 2030, heat stress could eliminate the equivalent of. At the same time, renewable energy already supported approximately Those figures reveal two sides of the same transformation. Climate change is already damaging workers' health and productivity. Climate action, meanwhile, can generate new employment and economic opportunities. But neither outcome is distributed equally. Without deliberate policies, the benefits of new industries may accumulate among investors and highly skilled workers while vulnerable communities bear the costs of transition. The ILO's framework emphasizes worker participation, social dialogue, collective bargaining, skills development, and decent work. The lesson is particularly important in countries where climate policy is routinely framed as a choice between protecting jobs and protecting the environment. That is a false choice. The real challenge is designing policies that protect both workers and the planet. 6\. Water connects nearly every dimension of the climate crisis. With guests from , we examined the climate crisis through a resource so fundamental that nearly every human activity depends on it: Water. Climate change is altering when precipitation falls, how intensely it falls, where water is stored, and how reliably communities can access it. Some regions face increasingly severe droughts. Others experience destructive flooding. Many experience both. Glaciers and mountain snowpack, which provide seasonal freshwater supplies to millions of people, are changing rapidly. Rising seas threaten coastal aquifers with saltwater intrusion. And extreme weather can overwhelm water treatment systems, damage sanitation infrastructure, and increase exposure to waterborne disease. discussed in Geneva involved the recent destructive flooding caused by glacial melt in the Himalayan mountains, causing more than 1,000 deaths in Nepal and Tibet. The broader lesson was that climate impacts do not respect the boundaries we draw between sectors or political jurisdictions. A mountain glacier affects a river. A river affects a reservoir. A reservoir affects agriculture, electricity generation, drinking water, and public health. The people making decisions about each of those systems may work in entirely different institutions. This is one reason UN-Water exists as a coordination mechanism across the UN system. And it is why water security must become central to climate adaptation rather than treated as a secondary environmental issue. At COP31, , an international initiative connecting climate policy, finance, and water management. The challenge is no longer simply understanding the hydrological consequences of climate change -- it is ensuring that water governance, infrastructure investment, and climate policy respond to those consequences together. 7\. Technology can help solve the crisis. It can also make it worse. One of the more interesting sessions during the week examined the growing role of digital technology and artificial intelligence in climate action. Digital systems can improve weather forecasting, support early warnings, optimize energy networks, monitor environmental changes, and strengthen disaster response. Satellite observations and advanced computational models have already transformed our ability to understand the Earth system. But technology is not environmentally neutral. Data centers consume electricity and water. Manufacturing electronics requires minerals, energy, and industrial infrastructure. Digital devices generate growing quantities of electronic waste. Artificial intelligence adds another layer of complexity. Its computational demands can create new pressures on energy and water systems even as its applications promise greater efficiency elsewhere. This tension should be central to how governments evaluate emerging technologies. A technology that improves efficiency in one sector may still create substantial environmental costs through its infrastructure, supply chains, or rapid expansion. The relevant question is not whether AI is inherently good or bad for the climate. It is whether particular applications deliver measurable environmental and social benefits that outweigh their full lifecycle costs. The same principle applies to corporate sustainability claims. In our sessions on environmental, social, and governance reporting, we examined how companies disclose their environmental performance, and how those disclosures can obscure as much as they reveal. A corporation may publish an attractive sustainability report while its core business model continues to depend on environmentally destructive practices. Transparency is essential, but disclosure is not the same thing as accountability. And neither is a substitute for measurable emissions reductions. 8\. Climate change is part of a larger planetary crisis. One of the most important ideas presented by was that climate change cannot be separated from biodiversity loss and pollution. Together, these form what the UN calls the Deforestation contributes to climate change while destroying habitats and weakening ecosystems that store carbon and regulate water. Pollution damages human health and biodiversity while imposing enormous economic costs. Resource extraction can accelerate environmental degradation even when the resulting materials are used in technologies intended to reduce emissions. This is why climate solutions must be evaluated as parts of larger systems. Replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy is essential. But an energy transition that ignores destructive mining practices, resource consumption, labor exploitation, and ecological damage risks reproducing other dimensions of the crisis. The discussions on circular economies, sustainable procurement, and systems thinking emphasized reducing waste, improving resource efficiency, and designing economic activity around ecological limits. The ultimate goal is not simply to preserve today's patterns of consumption while changing the technologies that power them -- it is to build economies capable of supporting human well-being without continually degrading the natural systems on which that well-being depends. 9\. International climate agreements are only as powerful as their implementation. During the session, we examined the architecture of international climate governance. The established the foundation for global cooperation. The 1997 binding emissions targets for certain developed countries. The created a broader framework in which countries submit and periodically strengthen their national climate commitments. One principle runs throughout these agreements: common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. In practical terms, countries share responsibility for confronting climate change, but they have not contributed equally to the problem and do not possess equal resources to address it. This principle is fundamental to international climate negotiations. It is also a source of persistent political conflict. Countries disagree over how much they should reduce emissions, who should pay for adaptation, how historical responsibility should influence present obligations, and what mechanisms should exist to ensure accountability. Meanwhile, the atmosphere continues accumulating greenhouse gases. The latest makes the implementation problem painfully clear. Even full implementation of existing national commitments would leave the world on a dangerous warming trajectory. At COP31, negotiators are debating how to strengthen mitigation, adaptation, financing, and the mechanisms used to evaluate progress. But agreements alone do not cool the planet. Emissions reductions do. And the distance between diplomatic promises and physical outcomes is where the future of climate policy will be decided. 10\. The biggest lesson from Geneva: We know far more than we are willing to do. One of the questions posed to us during the programme was what we intended to do with the knowledge we gained. It is a question that deserves to be asked of governments, corporations, and international institutions as well. What happens after the conference ends? After the speeches, presentations, negotiations, and photographs? After the next set of commitments is announced? I left Geneva with a deeper appreciation for the extraordinary expertise distributed throughout the UN system. Scientists are monitoring changes in the Earth system with remarkable precision. Disaster specialists understand how to reduce exposure and vulnerability. Economists are developing mechanisms to finance resilience. Human rights experts are identifying legal responsibilities. Labor specialists are designing frameworks for equitable transitions. Engineers and technology experts are developing practical tools for reducing emissions and protecting communities. None of these disciplines can solve the crisis alone. That was perhaps the most consistent lesson across the programme. Climate change is not simply a problem of atmospheric chemistry. It is a problem of energy, economics, governance, public health, human rights, infrastructure, and political power. The challenge is not a shortage of knowledge, but rather the failure to translate that knowledge into coordinated, adequately financed, enforceable action. As COP31 continues in Turkiye, governments have another opportunity to narrow the distance between what they know and what they do. But the atmosphere does not negotiate. The oceans do not recognize political boundaries. And communities facing deadly heat, rising seas, and destructive storms cannot wait for another decade of incremental promises. The people I met in Geneva are working on different parts of an extraordinarily complex problem. Their work matters. But the ultimate measure of success will not be how many conferences are held, how many reports are published, or how many commitments are announced. It will be whether emissions fall, whether ecosystems recover, whether vulnerable communities become safer, and whether governments finally accept responsibility for the future their decisions are creating. | | # [Your 2027 Medicare bill is being decided right now](https://theeagledispatch.podia.com/p/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJuZXdzbGV0dGVyX2xpbmtfaWQiOjQ2MzU5NzN9.ZonDTC7e383av8bbvCtfGHi6JjxzdzZj_l7LhGkIyHw/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdHVkZW50X2lkIjo2NjAzOTM5OSwibmV3c2xldHRlcl9pZCI6MzMxODkyN30.sjTSEf_TZhl_hcSd0mxI1VQg1IGtOxFrrcdHgpNVqXw)
---
|
---
#### **The December Deadline**
## **Three weeks to the Medicare deadline that locks in your 2027 costs**
_Most people on Medicare let their plan auto-renew, and that single habit can cost them hundreds next year. The window closes December 7._
The loudest money deadline of the season is not on Wall Street. It is in your mailbox.
---
Medicare open enrollment runs through December 7, and the choices a person makes by then set what they pay for health coverage all through 2027. Miss it, and you keep this year's plan whether it still fits or not.
The pieces are moving for next year. The CMS projects the average Medicare Advantage premium will [fall about 16.5 percent](https://theeagledispatch.podia.com/p/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJuZXdzbGV0dGVyX2xpbmtfaWQiOjQ2MzU5Njl9.EE6dOWHfItizr9yaM15t2w876KSrfawBlldQkpW8n2I/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdHVkZW50X2lkIjo2NjAzOTM5OSwibmV3c2xldHRlcl9pZCI6MzMxODkyN30.sjTSEf_TZhl_hcSd0mxI1VQg1IGtOxFrrcdHgpNVqXw), while the standard Part D drug deductible climbs from $615 to $700 and the yearly out-of-pocket drug cap rises to $2,400. Plans reshuffle their drug lists and pharmacies every year, so the plan that was a bargain in 2026 can turn into the wrong one for 2027.
Here is the part that stings. Part B premiums come straight out of a Social Security check, so even a solid [3.6 percent raise](https://theeagledispatch.podia.com/p/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJuZXdzbGV0dGVyX2xpbmtfaWQiOjQ2MzU5NzB9.QDDNQawC1Db6l9CUsR2RxpxbqY7ZCXI4Lkm2H2m9ZcY/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdHVkZW50X2lkIjo2NjAzOTM5OSwibmV3c2xldHRlcl9pZCI6MzMxODkyN30.sjTSEf_TZhl_hcSd0mxI1VQg1IGtOxFrrcdHgpNVqXw) for 2027 gets thinned before it ever lands.
The one lever most households truly control is the plan itself, and this is the only window to pull it. In my planning years I saw an afternoon of careful comparison pay for itself again and again.
---
#### **Before December 31**
## **The year-end money chores that are easy to forget and costly to skip**
Medicare is not the only clock running. A short list of money tasks expires with the calendar, and a few of them carry real penalties for missing the date.
---
▪ Required withdrawals. Anyone 73 or older generally must take their retirement-account distribution [by December 31](https://theeagledispatch.podia.com/p/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJuZXdzbGV0dGVyX2xpbmtfaWQiOjQ2MzU5NzF9.wBe9iSsPp-mnecwCmbNnUP1q7O1ZxAVyrjGcvibPX9I/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdHVkZW50X2lkIjo2NjAzOTM5OSwibmV3c2xldHRlcl9pZCI6MzMxODkyN30.sjTSEf_TZhl_hcSd0mxI1VQg1IGtOxFrrcdHgpNVqXw), and the penalty for missing it can run as high as 25 percent of the amount they should have taken.
▪ Tax-loss harvesting. After a jumpy few weeks in the market, selling a losing position before year-end can offset gains and trim a tax bill, as long as you respect the 30-day wash-sale rule.
▪ Charitable giving. Gifts made by December 31 count for this tax year, and those over 70 and a half can give straight from an IRA to help satisfy a required withdrawal tax-free.
▪ Flexible spending accounts. Many workplace FSA dollars vanish at year-end, so an unspent balance is worth checking before it simply disappears.
None of these are glamorous. They are the plain housekeeping that separates a tidy financial year from an expensive one, and every one of them shares the same deadline.
---
#### **One Number**
**15** is how many more prescription drugs get newly negotiated Medicare prices on January 1, [including Ozempic and Wegovy](https://theeagledispatch.podia.com/p/l/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJuZXdzbGV0dGVyX2xpbmtfaWQiOjQ2MzU5NzJ9.R9GtbwDoCjGd5Z5oRTamv-x82VT76APUQ08vX9U5zio/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdHVkZW50X2lkIjo2NjAzOTM5OSwibmV3c2xldHRlcl9pZCI6MzMxODkyN30.sjTSEf_TZhl_hcSd0mxI1VQg1IGtOxFrrcdHgpNVqXw), along with treatments for cancer, asthma and diabetes. For the millions who take them, the price at the pharmacy counter is about to change. It is one more reason the plan picked before December 7 deserves a careful look this year instead of a rubber stamp.
#### **Why I Led Here**
I led with Medicare because it is one of the few money decisions where doing the homework reliably pays, and the deadline is close enough to act on this week. It is also the one that tripped up the most good, careful people I ever sat down with.
The deadline is not the enemy here. The drawer is. A plan notice arrives looking like junk mail, it gets set aside, and by the time anyone looks again the window has closed for another year. I have watched one overlooked letter cost a good family a better plan more than once. An afternoon with the plan finder before December 7 is some of the best-paid work a household can do all winter.

Anyone who’s spent time on the water in Hampton Roads knows that the tide always turns.
Four years ago, I lost this seat. I didn’t second-guess the fight then, and I’m glad I didn’t.
On November 3rd, the tide turned.
The people of Hampton Roads sent me back to Congress. And we weren’t alone. Across the country, voters delivered a blue wave that flipped the House with what’s on track to be the largest Democratic majority in decades. Democrats flipped Senate seats in places like Kansas, Texas, and Ohio to take back that chamber too.
All cycle, I said Democrats needed to flip just three House seats to take back the majority. We blew right past that number, and VA-02 was one of the seats that got us there.
I’m proud of that. I’m also not one to oversell, so here’s the plain truth about how we did it:
We spent down to zero.
When you’re in a Toss-Up race against an incumbent and a flood of outside money, you don’t hold anything in reserve. You leave it all on the deck.
Every dollar went into this victory. That was the right call. But it means that before I’m sworn in, we need to settle up.
